title: Partial RPC lease migration strands capacity in a durable reservation journal
fault_primitive: Transport admission writes SHA-1 lease identities to a Redis journal and occupancy index while the legacy pool completion adapter retires raw request identities
incident_class: Partial distributed semaphore schema migration with incompatible acquisition and completion protocols
symptoms: Ready frontend pods return HTTP 500 with Thrift connection timeout exceptions naming healthy RPC backends. Redis occupancy indexes reach 64 entries per upstream despite collapsed backend activity; a durable receipt journal restores indexes after they are cleared.
why_hard: The nginx connection pool shipped in the image remains intact. Acquisition occurs in worker-initialized transport code, separately from the completion adapter in master initialization. The release adapter looks successful because Redis ZREM/HDEL return zero without error. Removing the pool customization used by the earlier fixer leaves transport admission active and still saturated. Deleting occupancy indexes alone reconstitutes them from receipts. Both code stages and the actual Redis member identity must be correlated; pod restarts and Deployment rollback preserve the ConfigMap and shared state.
expected_agent_pitfalls: Follow connection timeout messages into healthy timeline services or network paths
Remove the pool completion adapter and assume the image pool disables distributed admission
Clear only rpc:sessions:* indexes and see them reappear from the reservation receipt journal
Fix SHA-1 normalization for new completions without retiring existing orphaned reservations
Restart, roll back or scale the frontend while retaining worker startup code and shared capacity
mitigation_summary: Remove both transport admission and legacy completion startup blocks from the existing nginx ConfigMap, replace frontend pods to load the image transport and pool, then delete only the two obsolete Redis reservation key families.

SAYS: The gateway’s Lua code is rejecting RPCs before they reach the backend services. Its Redis session limiter stores hashed reservation IDs but releases unhashed IDs, leaving stale reservations that exhaust the limit. I’ll remove the faulty limiter and restore direct Thrift connections.
